newsitem.title: USA: U.S. congressman proposes school prayer amendment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congressman proposes school prayer amendment.

text.p: A Republican congressman proposed on Monday an amendment to the U.S. Constitution aimed at allowing prayers in public schools, while opponents decried the measure as potentially harmful to minority religions.
Representative Ernest Istook of Oklahoma said he would introduce the 52-word "Religious Freedom Amendment" when Congress returned from spring recess.
"This is to restore the protection of our precious religious freedoms and liberties which have been eroded by a steady onslaught of court decisions," Istook said.

"Courts have gone far beyond outlawing prayer in many public school settings. They have aided a systematic campaign to strip religious symbols, references and heritage from the public stage ... This is our peaceful answer to that assault," Istook said.
He used examples of court orders to remove a cross from a San Francisco park, a display of the Ten Commandments from a courtroom and crosses from city seals.
There is currently no sponsor in the Senate for the measure, which must be approved by two-thirds of the House and Senate to pass and then by the legislatures of three-fourths of the States.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, and House Majority Leader Dick Armey, a Texas Republican, both wrote in support of Istook's effort.
The Rev. Barry Lynn, executive director of Americans United for Separation of Church and State, said the amendment could harm the interests of religious minorities.

He warned that it could spark efforts to declare the United States a Christian nation, allow students and teachers to select the time, place and manner of school prayer, and permit "every public place to become a religious bazaar."
It would also allow use of public funds for private religious schools and social service missions, he said.

Ralph Reed, executive director of the Christian Coalition, said passage of the religious amendment would be a top priority. He said the group planned to spend $1 million to $2 million for a campaign, to start on May 20, that will include radio ads and targeted voter mail.

The coalition of groups in opposition would make defeating the amendment a legislative priority, but would probably not have as much money backing its effort, Mark Pelavin, associate director of the Religious Action Centre of Reform Judaism, said.
"By claiming to protect the religious rights of all Americans it (amendment) would in fact greatly reduce the religious liberty we now possess," Pelavin said.
